top_news.title: Georgia Grants Recognition to Indian Students
top_news.summary: Georgia details MD graduates registration and practice rights for Indian families Georgia's quality authority has detailed how its six-year MD programme matches India's FMGL Regulations, 2021 - including the registration and right to practise that graduates receive. For roughly 20,000 Indian students enrolled in Georgian medical universities since 2021, recent questions about graduate practice rights have caused concern. A September reply by the National Medical Commission (NMC) to a grievance, circulated on social media with captions declaring the Georgian degree "invalid", triggered calls from anxious parents. On October 14, Georgia's National Center for Educational Quality Enhancement (NCEQE), the agency under the Ministry of Education, Science and Youth that accredits every medical programme in the country, published an updated 17-point statement explaining its position. What the FMGL Regulations require India's Foreign Medical Graduate Licentiate (FMGL) Regulations, notified on November 18, 2021, apply to Indians who enrolled in foreign medical schools after that date. Regulation 4 requires a course of at least 54 months; a 12-month internship in the same institution; English as the medium of instruction; and the subjects listed in Schedule I. Regulation 4(b) adds that the graduate must be registered with the regulatory body of the country of study, with a right to practise "at par" with that country's own citizens. After that come the FMGE (or NExT when introduced), a further supervised internship in India, and permanent registration. The NCEQE statement confirms that the MD programme comprises "no fewer than 360 ECTS credits" and "cannot be shorter than six academic years"; that "the sixth year is fully dedicated to a mandatory internship (internatura)" at the university's clinics and teaching hospitals; that in English-taught programmes "the entire teaching and learning process, including clinical training, is conducted in English"; and that the Schedule I subjects "are fully incorporated into the accredited one-cycle Medical Doctor programs in Georgia." The central question has been 4(b). Registration and the right to practise Under the Law of Georgia on Medical Practice, the statement says, MD graduates "are entitled, irrespective of their citizenship, to be employed as junior doctors". On request, the LEPL Regulation Agency for Medical and Pharmaceutical Activities - the State regulator for medical activity - issues a written confirmation to each graduate. "The official certificate from the LEPL Regulation Agency for Medical and Pharmaceutical Activities has individual (unique) registration number with right to practice," NCEQE states. For the "at par" test, the statement says Georgian and foreign graduates "have identical professional rights" and are equally entitled to hold a Junior Doctor (Junior Physician) position and receive remuneration. Nothing in the Georgian law distinguishes by nationality. Under Article 14, "a junior doctor may engage in independent medical practice where a patient is in a life-threatening condition or requires emergency medical care." Junior doctors "owe patients the same fundamental duties as physicians," and their role "is not limited to observation or assistance; within the scope of their professional knowledge and the limits prescribed by law, junior doctors perform clinical functions." articles.title: Georgia Grants Recognition to Indian Students
articles.summary: Georgia details MD graduates registration and practice rights for Indian families Georgia's quality authority has detailed how its six-year MD programme matches India's FMGL Regulations, 2021 - including the registration and right to practise that graduates receive. For roughly 20,000 Indian students enrolled in Georgian medical universities since 2021, recent questions about graduate practice rights have caused concern. A September reply by the National Medical Commission (NMC) to a grievance, circulated on social media with captions declaring the Georgian degree "invalid", triggered calls from anxious parents. On October 14, Georgia's National Center for Educational Quality Enhancement (NCEQE), the agency under the Ministry of Education, Science and Youth that accredits every medical programme in the country, published an updated 17-point statement explaining its position. What the FMGL Regulations require India's Foreign Medical Graduate Licentiate (FMGL) Regulations, notified on November 18, 2021, apply to Indians who enrolled in foreign medical schools after that date. Regulation 4 requires a course of at least 54 months; a 12-month internship in the same institution; English as the medium of instruction; and the subjects listed in Schedule I. Regulation 4(b) adds that the graduate must be registered with the regulatory body of the country of study, with a right to practise "at par" with that country's own citizens. After that come the FMGE (or NExT when introduced), a further supervised internship in India, and permanent registration. The NCEQE statement confirms that the MD programme comprises "no fewer than 360 ECTS credits" and "cannot be shorter than six academic years"; that "the sixth year is fully dedicated to a mandatory internship (internatura)" at the university's clinics and teaching hospitals; that in English-taught programmes "the entire teaching and learning process, including clinical training, is conducted in English"; and that the Schedule I subjects "are fully incorporated into the accredited one-cycle Medical Doctor programs in Georgia." The central question has been 4(b). Registration and the right to practise Under the Law of Georgia on Medical Practice, the statement says, MD graduates "are entitled, irrespective of their citizenship, to be employed as junior doctors". On request, the LEPL Regulation Agency for Medical and Pharmaceutical Activities - the State regulator for medical activity - issues a written confirmation to each graduate. "The official certificate from the LEPL Regulation Agency for Medical and Pharmaceutical Activities has individual (unique) registration number with right to practice," NCEQE states. For the "at par" test, the statement says Georgian and foreign graduates "have identical professional rights" and are equally entitled to hold a Junior Doctor (Junior Physician) position and receive remuneration. Nothing in the Georgian law distinguishes by nationality. Under Article 14, "a junior doctor may engage in independent medical practice where a patient is in a life-threatening condition or requires emergency medical care." Junior doctors "owe patients the same fundamental duties as physicians," and their role "is not limited to observation or assistance; within the scope of their professional knowledge and the limits prescribed by law, junior doctors perform clinical functions."
